summary:
The United Arab Emirates subjects trans visitors to gender-document screening at entry. In 2025, two Israeli trans women were detained for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, and denied entry with their passports confiscated.

Entry refusals on identity grounds are documented across a decade. In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was held for five hours at Dubai International Airport, denied entry because authorities did not recognise her gender as legitimate, and had her passport confiscated. In March 2022 the Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe runner-up, was stopped at Dubai immigration and interrogated for nine hours before being deported to Thailand ahead of her Expo 2020 appearance; her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

The legal framework underpinning these encounters explicitly acknowledges and penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles. A Cairo 52 legal review finds that transgender expression and unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion. Under Article 412(2) of the federal crimes law enacted in 2021, men who disguise themselves as women in order to enter a women-only space may be imprisoned for up to one year and fined up to AED 10,000; this replaced a broader previous prohibition on clothing 'inappropriate for one's sex'.

Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the same law, carrying a minimum of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed; the federal criminal code enacted in early 2022 introduced this provision. Article 409(5) permits an action only on the complaint of a spouse or guardian of the complainant, who may withdraw it. Because civil guardianship ends at 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual male-male conduct between adults, so federal prosecution is not possible in that case; for female-female relations a married woman's husband, or under the Islamic wali concept an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative, may qualify, so prosecution remains possible where such a complainant exists. Article 409 also covers unmarried different-sex couples.

The UAE does not recognise same-sex marriage and provides no legal gender recognition. No UAE law or policy prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and LGBTI organisations cannot register; no LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organisation operates openly anywhere in the country.

Trans foreigners in custody face additional hazards. Reports of mistreatment in detention tied to suspected or established same-sex conduct include beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture. Detainees have been held in cells designated for 'effeminate' people. Involuntary medical and psychological treatment, including hormonal therapy and detention for forced psychological treatment, has occurred in connection with suspected or established same-sex conduct. Sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances. Gay conversion practices are not prohibited or discouraged by any law or regulation.

Trans people have been arrested for presentation alone. In December 2013 two Brazilian transgender women who called police about prejudice they had witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for 'imitating women', held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported. In 2005 a raid on an Abu Dhabi desert resort targeting 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a 'gay wedding' ended with 12 convictions, 11 five-year sentences and one one-year sentence, with initial reports that some defendants were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences.

A Brazilian trans woman detained in the UAE from September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, publicly accused the Brazilian consulate of negligence, a case illustrating prolonged custody and limited consular protection for trans foreigners.
tangentialFactors:
State hostility is expressed through information control as well as enforcement. The country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word 'gay' or 'sex'. The Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 for depicting a same-sex relationship and banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' transgender flag. The Arabic children's comic Majid came under investigation in 2022, with an edition withdrawn over dialogue using the Arabic word مثلي (mithli). In June 2023 Amazon blocked 150 search terms including 'lgbtq', 'pride' and 'closeted gay' on its UAE site under threat of penalties, removing listings that included Roxane Gay's Bad Feminist.

Officials have publicly declared there is 'no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE'. The pop group Steps refused a Dubai show in June 2023 over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality, an indication of the disclosure conditions applied to performers.

Police action against same-sex conduct includes a 2012 raid breaking up a party of 30 men in Dubai and the arrest that year of two Indian men for consensual sex in a public toilet, each receiving six months plus deportation. In July 2007 in Dubai, a 16-year-old French-Swiss boy who was kidnapped and raped was initially treated by police as a suspect; fear of prosecution under Article 177 drove him and his family to leave the country, although he was later awarded AED 15 million (US$4 million) in civil compensation. A 17-year-old acquaintance was implicated in luring him, and the family accused UAE authorities of failing to notify them that one of the rapists was HIV-positive, delaying medical attention.

Youth are directly criminalised and vulnerable. The country ranked 85th with a score of 37 on PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index, a dated measure of low reported wellbeing.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, so identity documents remain inconsistent with lived gender indefinitely and every domestic check-point, hospital registration or bank interaction carries the same document-mismatch exposure described for visitors. Article 412(2) narrows the presentation offence to disguising oneself as a woman to enter a women-only space, replacing the earlier broader ban on clothing 'inappropriate for one's sex', but the exposure is to spaces rather than to dress in public generally.

Article 409's complaint requirement shapes who can be prosecuted. Consensual male-male conduct between adults cannot be federally prosecuted for want of an eligible complainant, whereas for female-female relations a married woman's husband, or an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative acting as wali, may qualify. Charges require a complaint basis.

No formal LGBTQ organisations or venues exist in Dubai; a nightclub that had sponsored a special night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government. Social attitudes and the likelihood of state repression prevent organisations or community education from forming. No law prohibits conversion practices, and no anti-discrimination protection exists on any protected ground relevant to gender identity or sex characteristics.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the gender-document screening reported by the 2025 entrants is a written border procedure or an ad hoc practice at Dubai airport is unresolved in the sources available here; the evidence consists of three individual accounts spanning 2016, 2022 and 2025 rather than a published entry rule.

The outcome of the Brazilian trans woman's detention, begun in September 2022, and the substance of her negligence allegation against the consulate are not established in the sources reviewed; the case is documented as an accusation and a period of custody.

The enforcement reach of Article 412(2) after it replaced the broader cross-dressing prohibition is not sourced, including whether presentation alone outside a women-only space can still attract charges under other provisions. The current treatment of the 2013 'imitating women' charge category is likewise unresolved beyond that case.

The status of the AED 15 million compensation awarded in the 2007 Dubai case on appeal or in payment is unresolved. Claims about site blocking and Amazon search-term suppression rely on reporting current to June 2023 and were not re-verified.
